title: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
summary: An array is the simplest data structure there is: elements side by side, with no gaps and no bookkeeping. Element `i` is at the start address plus `i` times the element size. Two-dimensional data such as a tile map is stored the same way, one row after another. This lesson shows the arithmetic, why the order you loop in matters for speed, and how games store grids.
ideas:
- Change `TileMap` to print the index of each tile instead of the tile, to see the flat numbering.
- Add a function `countAround(x, y, c)` to `TileMap` that counts how many of the eight neighbouring tiles equal `c`, skipping any outside the map. That is the practice task, in a slightly different form.
- In Visual Studio, look at `map.tiles.data()` in the Memory window and find the `@` (`0x40`) and `>` (`0x3E`).

cards.q: How is the address of `a[i]` worked out?
cards.a:
The address of `a[0]` plus `i` times the size of one element

Array elements sit side by side with nothing between them, so the arithmetic is all it takes.

Each complete row is stored after the previous one, so (row, column) is at row × width + column

Built-in two-dimensional arrays in C++ are row-major. Column × height + row would be column-major, the other order.

cards.q: Why does loop order affect speed over a big grid?
cards.a:
Rows use each 64-byte cache line fully; columns fetch a new line each step

Same number of elements, very different number of cache-line fetches. Make the inner loop walk along rows for a row-major grid.

cards.q: An array of `double` starts at address `0x1000`. Where is element 3?
A tile map is 10 wide and stored row-major. Which index holds the tile at x = 3, y = 2?
Which loop order is faster for a large row-major grid?
cards.a:
Rows in the outer loop, columns in the inner loop

The inner loop should walk through memory in order, so each cache line fetched is fully used.

cards.q: Inside `void f(int a[])`, what is `sizeof(a)` on x64?
cards.a:
8, the size of a pointer

An array parameter is really a pointer. The length is not passed.
